candidate_analysis.explanation: The Random Forest assigned a MALWARE probability of only 0.6150, which is modest. All 20 top n-grams push toward cryptojacking, but their SHAP contributions are small and tightly clustered (+0.0050 to +0.0093), with no dominant feature. The evidence does not include function names, API calls, or per-function locations, so nothing ties these patterns to mining behavior. Most of the high-frequency n-grams are stack and call-convention patterns: CALL PUSH (0.013407, +0.009305), LEA PUSH (0.011528), ADD PUSH (0.010809), POP PUSH (0.010317), MOV PUSH (0.055935), SUB PUSH (0.004440) and POP CALL (0.003178). These are typical of 32-bit cdecl compiled code and are common in benign binaries, so their positive SHAP values more likely reflect how the model was trained than any mining-specific logic. Some rarer n-grams are more suggestive of numeric or bit-manipulation work: SUB SBB, SBB INC, SHRD SHR and CDQ MOV (multi-precision or 64-bit arithmetic on a 32-bit target), POP XOR, and FSTP MOV and ADD CVTSI2SD (floating-point conversion). Multi-precision arithmetic can occur in hashing or cryptographic code, but it also occurs in ordinary math, runtime and library routines. These n-grams have very low frequencies (0.000013 to 0.000353), so they are weak indicators. MOV MOVSD.REP suggests block memory copying, which is generic. Overall the evidence is consistent with a malware lean but is inconclusive, and it lacks the strong, concentrated crypto-primitive signatures (such as rotate/XOR/shift-heavy hash loops) needed for high confidence.

Borrow and increment arithmetic, again suggesting multi-precision operations. Very rare (0.000063) and ambiguous.
Typical stack and argument manipulation in compiled code. Frequent and generic.
Register save and restore or stack shuffling. Generic compiler or runtime behavior.
Call sequence following a stack restore, such as a thunk or PIC-style call. Generic, not mining-specific.
x87 floating-point store followed by a move. Extremely rare (0.000013). It indicates some floating-point usage but not a specific mining routine.
A pop followed by an XOR, possibly register zeroing or simple mixing. Weak on its own, though XOR is common in crypto and hash code.
Stack restore followed by arithmetic. Generic, with low frequency (0.000353).
Address computation for an argument before a call. Standard compiled code.
Double-precision shift followed by a shift, used for 64-bit shifts on 32-bit x86. It could occur in hashing or bignum code but is also common in generic runtime helpers. Very rare.
Stack restore followed by address computation. Generic and very rare.
Zero-extension of a byte or word followed by a push, typical of character or byte handling. Not specific to mining.

Push followed by a bitmask operation. Weakly suggestive of bit manipulation, but ambiguous.
Integer-to-double conversion after an add, indicating floating-point computation. Extremely rare (0.000013) and not diagnostic.
Register restore followed by a move. Generic function epilogue behavior.
Most frequent n-gram (0.0559), basic argument setup. Its SHAP value is the lowest of the top 20 and it carries little cryptojacking-specific meaning.
